s: B. Privacy, autonomy and family.
Family and child-rearing.

Parents have a fundamental right to direct the upbringing and education of their children: Meyer v. Nebraska (1923, foreign-language instruction), Pierce v. Society of Sisters (1925, private schools), and Troxel v. Granville (2000, grandparent visitation).
The family includes extended family (Moore v. City of East Cleveland, 1977).
Marriage.
Loving (1967) protected interracial marriage.
Zablocki v. Redhail (1978) struck a requirement that fathers behind on child support obtain court permission to marry.
Turner v. Safley (1987) protected prisoners' right to marry, and Obergefell (2015) extended the right to same-sex couples.
Contraception and procreation.
Skinner v. Oklahoma (1942) struck compulsory sterilization of certain criminals on equal protection grounds.
Griswold v. Connecticut (1965) protected married couples' use of contraception through "penumbras" of specific guarantees, and Eisenstadt v. Baird (1972) extended that to unmarried persons.
Intimate conduct.
Lawrence v. Texas (2003) overruled Bowers v. Hardwick (1986) and struck criminal sodomy bans.
Abortion.
Roe v. Wade (1973) recognized a right to abortion with a trimester framework.
Planned Parenthood v. Casey (1992) reaffirmed its "central holding" under an undue-burden standard.
Dobbs v. Jackson Women's Health Organization (2022) overruled both.

It held that the Constitution confers no right to abortion because the right is not deeply rooted in history and tradition, and returned the issue to legislatures, where regulation receives rational-basis review.
The majority stated that its decision does not cast doubt on other precedents.
Justice Thomas's concurrence urged reconsidering all substantive due process precedents.
Right to refuse treatment.
Cruzan (1990) assumed a competent person's right to refuse lifesaving treatment and permitted a clear-and-convincing evidence requirement.
Glucksberg (1997) found no right to physician-assisted suicide.
